newsitem.title: USA: Rough seas ahead for some U.S. ports.
newsitem.headline: Rough seas ahead for some U.S. ports.

text.p: Unless U.S. harbors adapt to the rapid evolution of freight transportation, they risk losing jobs and market share to more aggressive ports throughout North America, warned industry representatives at a conference here this week.
Coastal ports in the U.S. can no longer count on the presence of large consumer markets in their backyards to attract carriers' business.

Instead, the advent of newer and larger container ships, the expansion of intermodally-based freight transportation and the growing popularity of global "alliances" among shipping lines mean ports must compete for an ever-shrinking pool of customers.

"American ports are being squeezed on both ends by their clients," said Charles Emerich, who follows the transport sector for Moody's Investor Services. "Competition among neighboring ports will intensify as they compete for each other's carriers."
His remarks were echoed by a number of maritime professionals who spoke at the Transportation Research Board's annual meeting this week.

With more carriers seeking to form partnerships and vessel-sharing agreements, ports have fewer operators lining up to do business. A link-up between the Danish shipping line Maersk and CSX-owned Sea-Land, was frequently-cited as an example of the new ways carriers are gaining leverage over ports.

In all likelihood, Emerich said, the consolidation that is occurring in the industry will bring about a "shake-out period" for some of the more vulnerable ports. Most susceptible to the fluctuations of the marketplace will be those ports that rely on one particular commodity, carrier or railroad for much of their business.
As shippers turn to larger vessels to transport their cargo, enabling them to reduce the number of voyages they make, they have become increasingly selective in choosing which ports to call on.
At the same time, rapid growth in global commerce means that some ports are handling an even greater amount of cargo.
"The bad news is, the customer base is shrinking," said James Brennan, a consultant for the maritime industry.
"The worse news is that the demands being placed on the ports to continue to survive are doubling or tripling over what they were as little as five years ago," he added.

On trans-Atlantic routes between Europe and North America, the average size of a container vessel is likely to increase over the next decade from 2,700 teu's (twenty-foot equivalent units) to 5,000-6,000 teu's, he said.

This next wave of so-called mega-container ships is being closely watched by port officials everywhere, but by none more so than in New York, where naturally shallow harbors must be continually dredged to accommodate ocean-going ships.
In the past few years, the Port of New York and New Jersey, the largest on the U.S. East Coast, has seen its market share squeezed by North Atlantic rivals such as Halifax and Norfolk.

"We see more and more cargo diverted to other ports and redistributed to our area (by truck and rail)," said Lillian Borrone, the director of port commerce at the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. "Right now, we're in jeopardy...If we don't get the channels that we need, we will become a regional port."

As the first port of call in the North Atlantic from Europe, Halifax is in the best position to take in cargo volumes coming from Europe, she said. Norfolk, on the other hand, would become more attractive to vessels arriving from Southeast Asia.

Borrone suggested that as an alternative to waging costly battles with each other for business, ports might some day decide to form alliances of their own in which neighboring harbors agree to focus on a particular commodity or type of service.
Philadelphia, she noted, has developed into a niche port for products such as cocoa, fruit and steel.
And with state and local funds becoming more scarce, ports will face increasing pressure to concetrate on what they do best.

"Fiscal constraints facing this country are likely to get worse before they get better, and that has major implications for the port industry," said Brennan. "We will clearly have to do more with less."
